content: Cystic fibrosis is a severe, life-limiting genetic disorder that affects approximately one in 2,500 newborns in the UK and an estimated 70,000 individuals globally, including both children and adults. This condition is complex and impacts multiple organ systems, with the respiratory system being particularly vulnerable. The disease is characterized by the accumulation of thick mucus in the airways, which predisposes individuals to recurrent infections and progressive lung damage. Inhaled bronchodilators are commonly prescribed to approximately 80% of individuals with cystic fibrosis to help open the airways and alleviate respiratory symptoms. These medications are available in both short-acting and long-acting formulations. Short-acting bronchodilators, such as muscarinic antagonists, act within minutes and provide relief for four to eight hours. Long-acting bronchodilators, on the other hand, also take effect quickly but maintain their therapeutic effects for approximately 12 hours or longer. This review focuses specifically on long-acting inhaled bronchodilators, as it replaces a previous review that included both shortand long-acting agents. However, due to the limited availability of research in this area, further updates to this review are not anticipated. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of long-acting inhaled bronchodilators in children and adults with cystic fibrosis. Additionally, the review aimed to identify the optimal drug and dosage regimen, if possible. To gather relevant data, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes information from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. The last search of this register was conducted on October 10, 2017. A separate search of the Embase database and reference lists of included trials was also performed, with the last search date being October 11, 2017. Clinical trial registries were reviewed for ongoing studies, and pharmaceutical companies were contacted to identify any additional trials. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized parallel trials that compared long-acting inhaled bronchodilators (including beta-2 agonists and muscarinic antagonists) with placebo, no treatment, or another long-acting bronchodilator in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility of trials based on their titles, abstracts, and full texts. They also evaluated the quality and risk of bias of the included studies and extracted relevant data. Any disagreements were resolved by consulting a third party. The search process identified 195 unique references. Of these, 155 were excluded based on their titles and abstracts. The full texts of the remaining references were reviewed, leading to the exclusion of 16 trials (28 references) and the inclusion of four trials (12 references) involving a total of 1,082 participants. One small trial (n = 16) evaluated the effects of beta-2 agonists and reported an improvement in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) after one month of treatment. However, the trial was judged to have an unclear risk of bias, and the quality of evidence was deemed very low. This trial did not report on patient-reported outcomes, quality of life, or adverse events. Three larger trials (n = 1,066) investigated the effects of the muscarinic antagonist tiotropium at doses of 2.5 µg and 5.0 µg over both short-term (up to 28 days) and longer-term (up to three months) periods. Only one of these trials reported changes in FEV1 after 28 days of treatment, showing no significant difference between the treatment and placebo groups. For the 2.5 µg dose of tiotropium, the mean difference (MD) in FEV1 was -0.02 liters (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.13 to 0.09), while for the 5.0 µg dose, the MD was 0.00 liters (95% CI -0.10 to 0.10). The evidence for these findings was of moderate quality. Adverse events were reported in all three trials and were found to be similar between the tiotropium and placebo groups. For the 2.5 µg dose, the risk ratio (RR) for adverse events was 1.01 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.11), and for the 5.0 µg dose, the RR was 0.98 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.06). Limited data were available on patient-reported outcomes and quality of life. Two of the trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias, while the third trial had an unclear risk of bias. In conclusion, neither long-acting beta-2 agonists nor long-acting muscarinic antagonists demonstrated significant improvements in the primary outcome of FEV1. No differences were observed between the intervention and placebo groups in terms of quality of life or adverse events. The quality of evidence supporting the use of beta-2 agonists was very low. While long-acting inhaled bronchodilators may reduce the treatment burden for individuals with cystic fibrosis by requiring less frequent administration compared to short-acting bronchodilators, future research should focus on evaluating their long-term effects on spirometric outcomes, quality of life, and adverse events.
